work.title: Thusnelde. Ein Singspiel in vier Aufzügen

history.p:
Encouraged by his acquaintance, the renowned author and theatre critic Johann Christoph Gottsched, Scheibe started working on another opera, though his first one ‘Artaban’ of 1738 had not been very successful. He began on the project already in 1740 and spent much time on both producing a usable text as well as composing the music. In a couple of letters which Scheibe wrote to Gottsched in February and April 1741, it is evident that he had given the opera some thought especially in terms of composing music to a tragedy as well as considerations regarding its framework. When the libretto was finished in 1749 he published it, including a thorough introduction to the history of opera as well as opera as a genre, which unfortunately is the only surviving complete source to the opera. In the introduction, Scheibe discusses the genre with numerous references to French and English practice. He also mentions that his libretto is based on an earlier text, 'Hermann', which he published. Unfortunately it has not been possible to find the printed text, but Scheibe's acquaintance Johann Elias Schlegel wrote a play ‘Herrmann, ein Trauerspiel’ which was finished in 1737. It is possible that Scheibe was inspired by Schlegel whose tragedy was published by Gottsched in his collection Die Deutsche Schaubühne (Leipzig 1743/48). Scheibe's introduction also deals with the history of opera and with the objections against the genre as well as containing a detailed summary of the opera’s plot. Contrary to the libretto of his first opera 'Artaban', the framework of which seems to have been more traditional, the present one has not been divided into recitative sections and arias; neither does the typography help the reader in determining the arias from the recitatives and ‘accompagnati’, suggesting that Scheibe consciously sought to obliterate the distinction. It is also evident that the choir sections are much more extensive in 'Thusnelde' than in 'Artaban', an approach he also discusses in the introduction.
There are no clear indications that the opera was staged though V.C. Ravn mentions that it was at least considered for performance in Copenhagen; unfortunately Ravn does not indicate from where he got the information. As soon as the libretto appeared in print, Scheibe started out revising the opera ‒ or at least the text ‒ so already the following year he included a list of corrections in his foreword to the translation of Holberg's Peder Paars, 1750 (SchW C4:011). At that time Scheibe and his family had moved to Sønderborg, in the southern part of Denmark where they established a music school for children. It seems improbable that Scheibe would have had time to promote a staging in Copenhagen of his most recent opera. In 1754 the libretto was thoroughly reviewed by Christian Gottfried Krause. As the reviewer, who wrote Von der musikalischen Poesie (1753), did not have access to the music, he therefore proposes how a composer might approach the various sections of the libretto in terms of setting it to music. It is tempting to suggest that Scheibe never composed the music to the opera. However, in 1764 when he published his first of three articles on the recitative (SchW C1:Coll.001), Scheibe includes an extensive music example of two-and-a-half pages from ‘Thusnelde’ to illustrate the distinction between recitative and accompagnato sections and the consequences for the declamation. He mentions that the example 'is taken from the author’s improved version of “Thusnelde"' (SchW C1:003, p. 228; music example appears on pp. 229–31). Perhaps Scheibe revised the opera taking into account Krause’s criticism. Finally, the printed libretto shelved in The Royal Library was Scheibe’s personal copy, and on it the composer has added the remark that the text has been completely revised. This might be the reason why the text to the accompagnato section is not found in Scheibe's 1749-version.
Scheibe’s ‘Thusnelde’ led to many discussions on German opera among the intellectuals of the day: it was considered to be the first proper German, national opera based on German ancient history in opposition to the Italian opera seria with its librettos in Italian on ancient Italian history. Thus Schmid writes in 1768: 'His "Thusnelde" is an attempt of an opera in the style of Metastasio with the difference that the composer has observed the three concepts [i.e. acting, time and place] strictly, a matter which in 1749 was still regarded a great achievement. If only the style’s poetry were stronger than that! However, the opera was composed in 1749.' It has been argued that Gluck’s revolutionary approach to composing operas was indeed inspired by Scheibe’s introduction.

annot.p: 'Ich bin jetzo nichts als eine juristische Grille. Doch aber ist mir heute was geschickt gekommen, daß HE. Haller eine Cantate auf den König George soll gemacht haben, die die Studenten in Göttingen aufgeführet. Ich lese es in einem Dinge: Thusnelde ein Singspiel, nebst einem Vorbericht von der Möglichkeit und Beschaffenheit guter Opern. Lesen Sie das Ding auch, bis meines herauskommt [i.e. Musikalische Poesie]. Ich will jetzo wieder darüber hergehen. Der Verfasser ist meiner Meynung, ich habe es aber noch nicht ganz gelesen'; quot. Gerhard Split, 'Zwischen Einverständnis und Kritik: Metastasio in der Opernpoetik Christian Gottfried Krauses', ed. Laurenz Lütteken & Gerhard Splitt, Metastasio im Deutschland: der Aufklärung (Tübingen, 2002), p. 158, n. 11.

annot.p: 'Seine Thusnelde ist ein Versuch einer Oper in Metastasios Geschmack mit dem Unterschied, daß der Verfasser die drey Einheiten strenger Beobachtet hat, ein Sache, die in 1749 noch für ein großes Verdienst gehalten ward. Wenn dafür die Poesie des Stils stärker wäre! Doch die Oper ist 1749 geschrieben.'

annot.p: 'Im Jahre 1749 unternahm er es, den damaligen Kunstrichtern zum Trotze, die aus allen Kräften gegen die Opern eiferten, durch seinen Singspiel, Thusnelde, die Möglichkeit einer deutschen regelmässigen Oper zu zeigen. Es wäre aber zu wünschen, dass der Verfasser aus andern Absichten, und mit grössern poetischen Talenten daran gegangen wäre.'

physDesc.physMedium: In 8o; front endpaper verso with shelf mark in pencil and library stamp, flyleaf, title page (sig. [A1r]), blank page with two library stamps, dedication (sig. [A2r]), blank page with one library stamp, dedicatory poem ('Singgedicht'; sig. [A3r]), blank page, title page to the introduction (Vorbericht') to the 'Singspiele' (sig. [A4r]), blank page, introduction ('Vorbericht'; sig. A5r (pp. [9]–76)), title page to 'Thusnelde' (p. [77]), list of characters (p. [78]), introduction ('Nöthige Vorerinnerungen'; pp. [79]–88), title page to Act One (p. [89]), blank page p. [90]), libretto (pp. [91]–167), engraving consisting of a hunter with a leashed dog barking at a sheep in a woodland (bottom of p. 167), blank page (sig. [L4v]), flyleaf. The source contains a few corrections and additions in ink by Scheibe (pp. 24, 29, 41, 51, 65, 74, 75, 89, 139, 163) thus implying that the source must have been his private copy.

Full leather binding with gilded boards and with paste-down of marbled paper, both front and back, gilded edges; paper of a good quality. The binding is similar to other works such as SchW C1:001 suggesting that they were part of Scheibe's private library.
